rationale: B wins because it keeps the market-test angle mostly inside the supplied facts: "A 9-million-customer UK bank tests whether its home playbook survives America" is usable. A's "Monzo re-enters a US challenger-bank market that already has three incumbents" smuggles in a competitor premise the update never gave it. B is not clean; "then spent it on a second shot at America" overclaims the profit link and needs a red pen. But A makes a whole kept angle stand on unsupported rivals, and that's scaffolding made of air.
gaps_in_A: "Monzo re-enters a US challenger-bank market that already has three incumbents" invents the competitive frame; the update supplies no Chime/Varo/Current facts or "three incumbents."
"Chime, Varo, Current, and similar" names rivals not in the supplied facts. External market knowledge belongs in proof gathering, not as a kept angle's foundation.
"Monzo is explicitly pairing its first-ever annual profit with a second US run" overstates sequence as intent; the update says both happened, not that Monzo paired them strategically.
"The prevailing assumption... is that a neobank needs its own national charter" needs outside evidence. Useful contrast, but don't sell a claimed industry consensus without proof.
gaps_in_B: "then spent it on a second shot at America" implies the profit funded the US relaunch. The update gives no spending, budget, or causation.
"renting a banking license" and "borrowed license" are punchy but legally loose. The grounded fact is a partner-bank arrangement, not a license lease.
"the US entry playbook has changed" is a trend claim that needs other cases. Right now Monzo is one case study.
"Any same-day news-peg angle" is overbroad. The launch itself is a same-day peg; the problem is fake external pegs.
